corpus_definition: an act that is illegal or that upsets or insults someone

forms.definition: a crime, or an action that hurts or insults people
forms.example: Driving without a licence is a serious offense.
forms.note: American spelling; British English writes offence. 'Take offense' means to feel upset by something.

syn.note: Easy word. A crime is always against the law; an offense can also be a small rule-breaking or an insult.
Formal: breaking a law or rule.
Formal: bad or illegal behaviour in general.
Related: words or actions that upset someone; only for the 'upset' part of this meaning.

forms.definition: to make someone feel upset or insulted
forms.example: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to offend you.
forms.note: In formal English it can also mean to break a law: 'people who offend again'.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word for making someone unhappy.
Stronger: you say or do something rude on purpose.
Related: 'hurt someone's feelings' is close to offend.

ant.note: To make someone happy, not upset.

forms.definition: rude in a way that makes people upset or angry
forms.example: Please don't use offensive words in class.
forms.note: As a noun, an offensive is a military attack; that is a different meaning.

syn.note: Easy word; offensive is stronger and more serious.
Very close: meant to make someone feel bad.
Making someone feel sad or upset, often about words.

ant.note: Not likely to upset anyone.
Showing good manners and respect.

forms.definition: upset because someone was rude or unkind to you
forms.example: She felt offended when nobody thanked her.

syn.note: Easy, general word for unhappy.
Close: your feelings are hurt.

forms.definition: in a rude way that makes people upset
forms.example: He behaved offensively at the party and had to leave.

syn.note: Easy word; offensively is stronger.

ant.note: In a way that shows good manners.

people.definition: a person who has broken the law
people.example: The young offender had to do community work.

context.text: Stealing is a serious offense in every country. My friend once made a joke about my city, but I wasn't offended. Still, some jokes can be offensive to other people.

reviewer_note: US spelling offense (UK offence) noted; offensive as noun (military attack) and the sports sense of offense left out as other meanings.

corpus_definition: Approved or agreed to by someone in a position of authority.

forms.definition: a room or building where people work at desks
forms.example: My mother works in an office in the city centre.
forms.note: Official is made from office, but office usually means a workplace, not 'approved by people in power'.

forms.definition: to be the person in charge at a ceremony or sports game
forms.example: A famous referee will officiate at the final.
forms.note: Belongs to official = a person in charge of an event, not 'approved'. Formal and not common.

forms.definition: approved or agreed by people in power
forms.example: He made an official announcement to the media.
forms.note: Also a noun: an official is a person with an important job in a government or organization.

syn.note: Easy word: someone in charge said yes to it.
Formal: given permission by people in power. British spelling: authorised.
Related: following the correct rules and style; not always approved by anyone.

ant.note: Not approved by people in power.
Relaxed, not following the usual rules.

forms.definition: in a way that is approved by people in power
forms.example: The new bridge was officially opened yesterday.

syn.note: Done in the correct, public way.

ant.note: Without approval from people in power.

context.text: The official exam results will come out next week. The new school in our district officially opens on 2 September.

reviewer_note: Noun 'an official' (person) has the same spelling as the headword, so it is explained in the adjective note instead of People & things.

corpus_definition: Inside a plane, ship, or train.
usage_note: be/get on board; on board + the plane/ship/train: 'on board the train to Bukhara'. 'Welcome on board' is common in announcements. Informal: 'be on board' also means to agree with a plan.

relations.note: Easy word, but general: inside any place, not only a plane or ship.
For ships: on land, not on the ship.

context.text: All passengers are now on board the train to Samarkand. There is a small café on board, so you can buy tea during the trip.

reviewer_note: Fixed phrase; informal 'agree with a plan' meaning only mentioned in usage_note.

corpus_definition: To make a machine work or control it.

forms.definition: the way a machine or system works or is controlled
forms.example: The operation of this machine is very simple.
forms.note: Very often it means a medical treatment where a doctor cuts the body (surgery).

syn.note: Easy: the running of a machine or business.
Formal: how well something works.
Related: the act of using a machine.

forms.definition: to make a machine work, or to work in a certain way
forms.example: She knows how to operate this heavy machine.
forms.note: Also means a doctor cutting the body to treat it: 'operate on a patient'.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word: 'use a machine'.
Common for machines and businesses: 'The machine runs on gas'.
Easy: 'How does this machine work?'
Formal: to work in the correct way.
Related: to decide how something moves or works.

forms.definition: working and ready to be used
forms.example: The new airport will be operational next year.

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Working in the way it should; a little formal.

ant.note: Not working because something is damaged.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with how something works or runs
forms.example: Operationally, the new system is much faster than the old one.

syn.note: Related: about real use, not ideas.

people.definition: a person whose job is to control a machine or system
people.example: The crane operator works high above the street.

context.text: My father operates a big machine at a factory in Navoi. The new production line will be operational next month, and he will train the new operators.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: two rows (make a machine work / work in a certain way) merged into one map because both corpus examples are about operating a machine; surgery sense only in notes.

corpus_definition: A person who believes that good things will happen.

forms.definition: a person who always expects good things to happen
forms.example: She is an optimist who always sees the bright side.

syn.note: Related: a person who believes the world can be perfect, sometimes not realistic.
Informal: a person with big hopes and plans that may not happen.

ant.note: A person who always expects bad things to happen.

forms.definition: the feeling that good things will happen in the future
forms.example: There is a lot of optimism about the new school.

syn.note: Easy word: wanting and expecting something good.
Related: feeling sure that things will go well.

ant.note: The feeling that bad things will happen.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family. Optimize (make something as good as possible) comes from the same Latin root but is not made from optimist.

forms.definition: expecting good things to happen
forms.example: I'm optimistic about my exam results.

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Everyday word: thinking about the good side.
Related: sure that something will go well.

ant.note: Expecting bad things to happen.
Thinking about the bad side of things.

forms.definition: in a hopeful way that expects good things
forms.example: She smiled optimistically before the race.

syn.note: Close, but hopefully also means 'I hope that': 'Hopefully it won't rain.'
Related: in a way that sees the good side.

ant.note: In a way that expects bad things.

context.text: My grandmother is a real optimist. Even in a cold winter she is optimistic and says spring will come soon. Her optimism helps the whole family.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry; optimize listed as not_family.

corpus_definition: Grown without the use of artificial chemicals.

forms.definition: a part of the body with a special job, like the heart
forms.example: The heart and the lungs are important organs.
forms.note: Organic comes from organ, but this belongs to organic = about living things and the body, not food grown without chemicals.

forms.definition: any living thing, such as a plant, animal or bacterium
forms.example: Very small organisms live in the soil.
forms.note: Belongs to organic = about living things (science), not food grown without chemicals.
There is no verb in this family. Organize comes from the same old root but means to plan or arrange things.

forms.definition: grown or made without artificial chemicals
forms.example: We only buy organic vegetables at the market.
forms.note: In science it also means 'coming from living things'.

syn.note: Easy word, but more general: natural food may still use some chemicals.
Informal: good for nature and the environment.

ant.note: Conventional farming is the usual kind that uses chemicals.

forms.definition: without using artificial chemicals
forms.example: These apples were grown organically in Fergana.

syn.note: Easy word, but more general.

context.text: My aunt has a small organic farm near Samarkand. She grows tomatoes organically, without any chemicals, and sells them at the bazaar.

reviewer_note: Organ and organism shown as other_meaning (body / living things); organize listed as not_family.

corpus_definition: Where something comes from or how it began.

forms.definition: the place where something comes from or the way it started
forms.example: He studied the origin of the language.
forms.note: Often plural for people: 'She is of Uzbek origin' / 'my family's origins'.

syn.note: The place or thing something comes from.
Easy word: the start of something.
Often plural: 'the roots of a problem', 'my roots'.
Easy word, but about time more than place.

ant.note: The origin is where something starts; the end is where it finishes.

forms.definition: the quality of being new, different and creative
forms.example: The judges liked the originality of her design.
forms.note: Belongs to original = new and creative, not where something comes from.

forms.definition: to start or come from a particular place or time
forms.example: Tea originated in China thousands of years ago.

syn.note: Easy, everyday way to say it.
Easy word: to start.
Easy word, very common.
Formal: used for problems or ideas that appear.

forms.definition: existing at the beginning, before any changes
forms.example: The original plan was to travel by train.
forms.note: Original also means new and creative, or not a copy: 'an original painting'.

syn.note: Easy word: 'my first idea'.
A little formal, very close.
The one that came before all others.

ant.note: The last one, after all the changes.

forms.definition: at the beginning, before something changed
forms.example: My family is originally from Bukhara.

syn.note: Easy phrase for the start of a situation.
Formal and very close.
Easy word, but often about order in a list.

ant.note: At the end, after a long time.

people.definition: the person who first had an idea or started something
people.example: She was the originator of the reading club.

context.text: My family is originally from Bukhara. The origin of our family name is Persian, and my grandfather still keeps the original papers.

reviewer_note: False-friend split: original = first (this meaning) vs new/creative (originality shown as other_meaning).

corpus_definition: A child whose parents have died.

forms.definition: a child whose mother and father are both dead
forms.example: The orphan found a new home with a kind family.

forms.definition: to make a child lose both parents
forms.example: He was orphaned at the age of five.
forms.note: Almost always passive: 'be orphaned'.

forms.definition: having no living mother or father
forms.example: The orphaned boy lived with his uncle in Andijan.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a home where children without parents live and are cared for
people.example: She grew up in an orphanage in Tashkent.

context.text: After the earthquake, many children were orphaned. An orphanage in the city gave every orphan food, clothes and a warm bed.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry; no true synonyms or antonyms exist, lists left empty.

corpus_definition: The final result of a process or event.

forms.definition: what happens at the end of a process or event
forms.example: We were happy with the final outcome.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with the same meaning.
A result of an action, often a bad one.
Easy word: the last part of something.
A change that something causes.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family. To talk about the result, people say 'turn out' or 'result in'.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Everyone waited for the outcome of the football match. In the end, the outcome was a draw, so both teams were happy.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; out- prefix not in the affix table, so no affix claimed.

corpus_definition: Located high up in the sky or above you.

forms.definition: the regular costs of running a business, like rent
forms.example: The shop moved to a smaller building to cut its overhead.
forms.note: Belongs to overhead = business costs, not 'above you'. British English usually says overheads.
There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: placed above your head, high up
forms.example: Please put your bag in the overhead locker.

syn.note: Easy word: far above the ground.
Formal: in the air or from the air.

ant.note: Under the ground: overhead cables hang in the air, underground cables are under the earth.

forms.definition: above your head, in the sky
forms.example: A bright plane flew overhead during the day.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word.
Literary: high up in the air.
Easy word, but more general.

ant.note: Lower than you, under you.
Under your feet, on the ground.

context.text: Birds flew overhead as we walked in the park. Later, on the plane to Tashkent, I put my bag in the overhead locker.

reviewer_note: Compound word; adjective is a conversion of the same spelling; business 'overhead(s)' shown as other_meaning.
